context_blurb:
Press two fingers to the inside of your wrist and feel your pulse, the push of each heartbeat. Heart, lungs, gut and kidneys work as one supply line, bringing every cell oxygen and food and carrying its wastes away. Doctors long got it wrong, until measuring set them right.

Galen, a Greek physician of the Roman Empire, taught that the liver turns food into blood, which the body's flesh then uses up. In his book of 1628, the English doctor William Harvey tested that idea with sums: a heart holding about two ounces of blood beats over a thousand times in half an hour, so even a little per beat adds up to more than the body's whole supply. Food eaten could never make that much blood so fast, so Harvey reasoned that the same blood must travel round the body in a circuit, again and again.

Harvey also bound a person's upper arm tight, and the veins below swelled, with little bumps marking the valves, one-way flaps inside them. Pressing on a swollen vein, he could push its blood up the arm toward the heart but never back down, because the valves open only toward the heart. So veins carry blood back to the heart. His teacher Hieronymus Fabricius had described the valves; Harvey showed what they are for.

The heart, a fist-sized double pump, has four chambers: two atria on top take blood in, and two ventricles beneath squeeze it out. The right ventricle sends blood only the short way to the lungs, but the left ventricle pumps blood out through the aorta to the whole body, so it must squeeze much harder, and its wall is roughly three times thicker than the right one's.

An artery is any vessel carrying blood away from the heart, and a vein any vessel bringing it back, whatever oxygen the blood holds. So the pulmonary artery, running to the lungs, carries oxygen-poor blood just back from the body, where the cells took its oxygen and gave it their carbon dioxide.

Harvey never saw how blood crosses from arteries to veins. In 1661 the Italian doctor Marcello Malpighi found the link by looking at a frog's lung through an early microscope: capillaries, vessels too fine for the naked eye. Blood trades with the body's cells in the capillaries because their walls are only one cell thick, thin enough for oxygen and food to pass out and carbon dioxide and wastes to pass in.

The lungs' air tubes end in the alveoli, hundreds of millions of air sacs wrapped in capillaries. Together the sacs' thin walls spread over 70 to 80 square metres, far more than a few big sacs could offer, and oxygen enters the blood only through that wall. Emphysema, most often caused by smoking, destroys the walls between sacs, so they merge into fewer, larger ones. With less surface left for oxygen to pass into the blood, each breath brings in less oxygen and the person runs short of breath, though the air is as rich as ever.

The small intestine takes in most of the food; the large intestine, about a metre and a half long, mainly takes water and salts back from what is left, returning about nine-tenths of that water to the blood, so the waste firms up. When a stomach bug rushes the waste through, there is no time to reclaim its water, so it comes out runny, one cause of diarrhoea; waste that lingers too long dries and hardens.

Each day the kidneys strain about a hundred and eighty litres of fluid from the blood, then take about ninety-nine percent of its water and useful substances back into the blood. What remains is urine, a litre or two a day, stored in the bladder: a little water carrying wastes such as urea, which the liver makes from broken-down proteins.

When both kidneys fail, wastes such as urea pile up in the blood and, untreated, can kill. Dialysis, first made to work by the Dutch doctor Willem Kolff in 1943, cleans the blood through a filter outside the body, usually three times a week.

Run hard up a hill and your pulse races, as your heart's output climbs to three or four times its resting flow. Nerves narrow the vessels of the kidneys and gut, cutting their blood by up to three-quarters, so the kidneys get less than at rest, while the working muscles' vessels open wide.
